title: The Right vs. The Right: Conservative “Liberals” in the Age of Trump
author: David S. D’Amato
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/The_Lincoln_Project_logo.svg-680x393.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/04/the-
right-vs-the-right-conservative-liberals-in-the-age-of-trump-2/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/The_Lincoln_Project_logo.svg-680x393.png)

The Lincoln Project logo - Fair Use

Before the last presidential election, [Adolph Reed Jr.
argued](https://www.thenation.com/article/politics/adolph-reed-biden/) that
“electoral politics has captured too much of the political imagination of the
American left—or, at least, of those occupying the cultural space that a left
would if there were one in this country.” Reed lamented the culturally
dominant “sensibility that approaches politics as largely performative, a
theater for the expression of righteousness, or bearing witness for justice
and against injustice.” As many radicals long predicted, this approach to
politics has handed the whole of the national political conversation to the
right, and this development will plague American society long after Trump is a
memory.

We’ve reached a point where [Bill Kristol can be a featured
speaker](https://x.com/UnPopulistMag/status/2078241778365280654) at a
“liberal” conference. It’s hard, in this context, to know which way is up, yet
we can see clearly that all ways now point rightward. Kristol is far from
alone; this cottage industry includes a who’s who of bloody-handed, Bush-era
conservatives who now pretend to care about the rule of law, when their whole
careers were spent writing thin apologies for the many constitutional
violations of the post-9/11 years. We would not be in this moment with MAGA
lawlessness and authoritarianism were it not for the people behind _The
Bulwark_ , the Lincoln Project, and the various other groups and outlets that
have emerged on the right since Trump.

In the Trump era, these self-congratulatory spaces have made a cottage
industry of rewarding demonstrably right-wing commentators for their empty
gestures in the direction of “democratic norms,” even as their old commitments
have gone unquestioned and largely remained intact. The predictable result is
that the political spectrum recognized by the mainstream of our culture and
politics has been dragged even further to the authoritarian, death-worshipping
and -dealing right. In this era, under these dynamics, the American right has
divided itself into a MAGA wing and an embarrassingly self-satisfied group of
supposedly noble, Never Trump conservatives, embraced by a cohort of lifeless
laptop liberals who largely share their still very conservative views. The
effect of this reconfiguration of the political right is to bring forth a
mainstream political spectrum that sits almost completely on the far right.

Media Matters for America’s [Craig Harrington
remarked](https://www.damemagazine.com/2022/07/11/mainstream-medias-rightward-
lurch/) on this baneful phenomenon back in 2022: “Even the supposedly liberal
outlets like MSNBC lurched to the right, soaking up castaway Republicans
guilty of Trump apostasy. After Biden won? The same outlets rushed to hire
more conservatives who jumped ship after January 6th.” It is possible to
imagine a liberalism that opposes war and empire, fights mass imprisonment and
the [wholesale destruction of the criminal
trial](https://www.law.georgetown.edu/legal-ethics-journal/blog/the-decrease-
in-trials-the-effect-on-competence/) and the rights of the defendant, fights
on behalf of working people, and meaningfully resists the police statism and
rampant warrantless surveillance of both the red and blue political teams. But
the “liberals” on offer today are generally not liberal in any substantive
sense; they instead use the terminology to signal their dislike for Trump.
Contempt for Trump has simply never been enough, absent any commitment at all
to genuinely liberal values. Policy endorsements and commitments continue to
be more important than vibes and self-serving self-descriptions.

It is telling that the reflex reaction (and it is reactionary) of Beltway and
elite “liberals” to Trumpism has been to sidle up to the most malignant and
discredited aspects of the neocon right. It is difficult to find any way to
reconcile all of the lovely liberal language with the policies of the war on
terror, long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, the brutalization of immigrants and
mass deportation, an increasingly militarized and repressive police state, and
rabid, unquestioning support of NATO and U.S. imperialism. The cheerleaders
for some of the worst and most globally destructive policies of our lifetimes
have been absorbed into and embraced by “liberals” completely without any
serious attempt to reckon with their records or careers. The entire political
axis apparently centers and turns on the person of Donald Trump. Opposition to
Trump means that one can be a committed illiberal, a warmongering, civil
liberties-destroying authoritarian, and still receive a warm reception amongst
professional liberals. They seem to believe it is the word “liberal” that
matters, not the substantive positions on issues. This has been deeply
troubling for those whose positions truly align with values of freedom and
equality. The practical upshot of these dynamics is that the “reasonable”
range of positions now runs from the hardcore right to the further extremes of
the right, with anything seriously anti-oligarchy, anti-empire, or anti-
carceral is treated as unacceptable and even un-American.

What the good-faith liberals aligning themselves with this reanimated corpse
of the neoconservative right seem not to understand is that these dynamics,
migrating the entire acceptable political spectrum firmly into the right, will
long outlast Donald Trump. In the end, Trump will have had two terms as
president. But the range of politically feasible options could remain bolted
down on the far right for many decades or even longer. It seems to be the case
that one of the reasons none of this can be challenged is because doing so
would force this coalition to admit that it is not in fact defending
liberalism in any deep sense. The driving force behind this phenomenon is a
reordering of elite consensus in order to insulate and perpetuate that
consensus. The absurd pretense of the “moderate” neocon as somehow a liberal
hides the rightward lurch Harrington identified several years ago.

What we see in the anti-Trump conservative coalition is a bit of sleight of
hand: the idea that rather than coming up with any real criticism of war,
extreme inequality and runaway corporate consolidation and power, prison
slavery, or the treatment of immigrants, we can simply revert to defending
elite institutions in their pre-Trump snapshot. Within this paradigm, it’s
easy to rehabilitate the loathsome Bush-era right without any critical
appraisal of their records of action. All of this perhaps shows that publicly
used ideological _labels_ can change much more rapidly than real policy
commitments, and that, particularly in our appearance-is-everything,
substance-is-nothing contemporary culture, the superficial label will be
accepted as signifying something real. No evidence is needed. In fact, the
bare label is strong enough to overcome mountains of evidence to the contrary.
This dynamic creates an optical illusion, the impression that the political
spectrum itself has not moved, despite the fact that it has been redefined and
pushed even further toward the authoritarian right.

Hating Trump cannot be enough to exonerate the conservatives who led us right
to him. Those on the real left should not confuse what we’re watching: a
struggle within and reorganization of the American right that is passing
itself off as the entire set of available options. All of these conservative
“liberals” remain committed to a version of corporate statism (read: fascism),
corporate welfare and extreme exploitation of labor, the unconstitutional
national security complex, and the idea that the U.S. should run the world
through military empire forever. They are not going to present a criticism of
the political-economic system itself, even as they may differ facially on
questions of manners, vibes, culture, and identity. This is what happens when
so-called liberals jettison any concern about actual, material inequality or
confronting the billionaire ruling class in favor of mere symbolism,
terminology, and jargon. “Liberal” conservatives in the age of Trump are never
going to challenge the foundations of the elite, big-city professional
political consensus.

The reality is that virtually all of what we associate with Trump predates him
by decades, if not much longer, and expanded under administrations the news
told you were liberal. There has been broad-based, two-party support for the
horrors we associate with Trump, or else it would have been impossible to get
Trump. We stand in a long historical process. If constitutionalism, democracy,
and the rule of law are taken to include strong protections for due process,
real separation of powers, and any conceivable limit on the powers of the
executive branch, then the bipartisan consensus has been much weaker than the
rhetoric of Never Trump conservative “liberals” wants you to know. Theirs is a
polite, boxed-in disagreement with MAGA over how extremely concentrated and
unaccountable power should operate at a narrow margin. What it is not is a
real debate about whether this kind of power is even desirable. Liberalism
might’ve gone in a different direction, and indeed it still could.

What we should have been discussing, particularly after 9/11, was the
frightening normalization of a security-administrative state that governs
completely outside of the Constitution’s three-party division and beyond the
reach of the Bill of Rights. If we had had the clarity and ethical temperament
to make this case, we might not be in a second Donald Trump administration
today. There were so many chances to open our eyes, but when Wikileaks, for
example, tried to get us there, the same conservative “liberals” made
themselves busy calling for the heads of government’s critics. We sat
dumbfounded as Washington handed more power to the imperial presidency,
centralizing the prerogatives of all three branches and reorganizing the state
around permanent coercive capacity. If anything, the language of
constitutionalism and the rule of law was deployed cynically to legitimate
this system rather than trying to hold it back.

Along these lines, the real social and political function of the conservative
“liberal” is to stabilize the political consensus of the ruling class and
their handlers in the Outer Party or the PMC. Their flowery rhetoric is a way
to launder the violence of the political-economic system. It is branding and
marketing for our captors. When the Never Trump conservatives wax poetic about
“our institutions,” they should be reminded that those are the institutions
that made a good “liberal” president claim the right to murder American
citizens anywhere in the world, with no charges or judicial process.
Conservatives who wring their hands over Trump’s fascism had no problem with
it for decades; their counterfeit anti-fascism leaves the structural state-
corporatism of the U.S. system insulated from criticism. Their embarrassing
respectability politics is one of fascism’s great historical defenses. Their
defenses of norms and institutions are the way our elites have always
disciplined the political discourse back into safe and comfortable channels
where empire and corporate looting can continue unabated.

In a [recent
post](https://bsky.app/profile/rechelon.bsky.social/post/3mquw4kwwhk2y), the
veteran PNW anarchist activist William Gillis distinguished between historical
forms of liberalism whose adherents “saw themselves in a grand historical
struggle between liberty and power” and a modern liberalism defined by
hostility to this older, more principled form, the “Party of Order” that
cynically passes for liberalism today. One of the tragedies of the Trump era
is the reduction of all mainstream liberalism to the latter, the Party of
Order, which is to say conservatism.
